vignette:
Malik, a 27-year-old African American man who drove for a living in a taxi and ride-share vehicle, came to treatment after months of feeling increasingly on edge in a way he could not explain to the people around him. He had grown up with a caregiver who used physical punishment that crossed into abuse, and he described childhood as a time when ordinary moments could turn suddenly dangerous. One of the clearest memories he carried was being grabbed by the arm and pressed against a rough surface while the room felt too hot, his skin registering the same unpleasant temperature he now recognized as instantly upsetting. He did not talk about the abuse in dramatic terms; instead, he described it as something his body remembered in flashes, especially when a particular texture brushed against him and when footsteps came up behind him without warning. In those moments, he was back in that earlier home, bracing for contact before he even turned around.

As a boy, Malik learned to stay alert to the sound of someone moving through the house, and that habit followed him into adulthood. Now, while waiting for fares or standing beside his car, he found himself tracking footsteps in parking lots, apartment corridors, and gas station lots with a vigilance that felt automatic. If he heard someone walking close behind him, his shoulders tightened and he would turn quickly, already preparing for something bad. He told himself that other people might say he was safe, but he could not make himself believe it. Even in places that were obviously public and familiar, he felt as though danger could arrive from just outside his field of vision, and he kept scanning until he was sure where everyone was. At work, this meant that in the airport queue, outside clubs, and on late-night streets, Malik was rarely fully settled. He watched mirrors more than he watched the road, and he checked the back seat often, not because there was anything specific there, but because not checking felt impossible.

Malik also noticed that his body seemed to respond before his mind had time to catch up. A cold draft against his forearm, the texture of a rough seat cover, or a hand brushing his skin in a crowded space could make him feel as though something was already wrong. He said, with visible frustration, that his body kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he knew, logically, that he was an adult in his own car or at home. That mismatch left him feeling permanently changed. He had come to believe that the abuse had altered him in a way he could not reverse, and he spoke about himself as though some damage had been set in motion long ago and was still there now. He also felt that he had lost his connection to his community and culture. He had once felt rooted in family gatherings and neighborhood life, but over time he pulled back from those spaces, telling himself he did not belong in the same way anymore. He attended less often, answered fewer invitations, and said that being around people who knew his family history made him feel exposed and separate.

To manage the discomfort, Malik began avoiding emotional closeness with others. He dated inconsistently and kept conversations surface-level, especially when someone seemed interested in getting to know him well. Intimacy felt risky to him, not because he wanted distance, but because closeness raised the possibility that another person could see how unsettled he was. When the pressure built, he distracted himself with whatever was available: music blasting in the car, scrolling on his phone between rides, staying busy with extra shifts, and sometimes taking drugs to shut the feeling down. He admitted that some of his choices put him at risk, including doing things that could hurt him if it meant not having to sit alone with his thoughts. In the past few months, he had found himself taking more chances than he used to, almost as if being in control of danger mattered more than avoiding it.

What finally brought Malik in was the way these patterns began interfering with both his work and his sense of himself. He was tired of feeling watchful every hour of the day, tired of flinching at footsteps behind him, and tired of needing to distract or numb himself just to get through a shift. He said he was not sure whether therapy could change anything, but he hoped it might help him feel less trapped inside his own body and less certain that he would always be altered by what happened to him. At the same time, he was most afraid that if he relaxed, even briefly, something would catch him off guard again.
